blog.l99.title: Lecturameter 1999: what would Lecturameter look like as an old PC program?
blog.l99.description: An alternative Lecturameter client with windows, menus, tables and an LCD timer, that opens your real backups. How it came about, what it has and what it leaves out on purpose. Coming free to Play Store and App Store.
blog.l99.og_description: An alternative Lecturameter client with windows, menus and an LCD timer, that opens your real backups. Coming free to Play Store and App Store.
blog.l99.tagline: An alternative Lecturameter client with windows, menus, tables and an LCD timer, that opens your real backups. How it came about, what it has and what it leaves out on purpose. Coming free to Play Store and App Store.
blog.l99.p_01: Lecturameter 1999 has been cooking for a few months. I have built it in pieces, here and there, without hurry and without a plan. I did not get serious about it until I saw that the iOS version was simpler than I expected and left me room to finish it.
blog.l99.p_02: It is not the only experiment. There are other Lecturameter universe projects in mind, some fairly advanced and others barely started. Most of them will probably never see the light.
blog.l99.p_03: It all started with an experiment I had been circling for a while.
blog.l99.p_04: The idea was to rebuild Lecturameter from scratch, several times, under radically different design premises. Without touching the real app and with no intention of replacing it. Seven versions came out. One imitated a 2016 Android app, another imagined what it would look like in 2036, another turned the library into a bookshelf with spines that get thicker as you read, another was designed for a handheld console with two screens.
blog.l99.p_05: The one I liked most was 1999. A late-nineties desktop program: dense, utilitarian, everything in windows, menus and tables. I decided to finish it, bit by bit, as a fun exercise and turn it into a complete client, with the real Lecturameter data underneath.
blog.l99.p_06: Lecturameter 1999 is a standalone app, separate from Lecturameter. When you open it you see a single maximized window over a teal desktop. At the top, the title bar and the menus: File, Edit, View, Session, Reports and Help. Below, a toolbar with pixelated icons. The central area is split in two: a tree with the library and a preview pane with the cover, and a table with one row per book. At the bottom, the status bar with the number of items, the total time and the book you are reading.
blog.l99.figcaption_01: The main window: tree, preview and table
blog.l99.figcaption_02: The timer, in its own window
blog.l99.figcaption_03: Minimized to the taskbar, still counting
blog.l99.p_07: This is the part that turns the experiment into something usable. Under the 1999 shell sits the real Lecturameter data model, copied as is: the same books, the same sessions, the same statuses, ratings and notes. The backup it exports is the same file Lecturameter exports, and the one it imports too.
blog.l99.p_08: In practice that means you can go to File, import your backup and see your whole library in a 1999 table. Read for a week with the LCD timer. Export. Go back to the modern app with the new sessions and without having lost a single field along the way. The Goodreads CSV goes in and out as well.
blog.l99.p_09: Book search is the same as in Lecturameter: it queries the app's own catalog and Google Books, and fills in title, author, pages, ISBN and cover. The cover is posterized and drawn without smoothing so it looks like a GIF from the time.
blog.l99.p_10: The reading flow is Lecturameter's, translated into windows. You select a book in the table and press the play button. The timer window opens, with a seven-segment display in green on black. You can move it, minimize it to a taskbar or close it: the time keeps counting in the status bar.
blog.l99.p_11: When you press stop, the save session dialog opens: date, minutes, first and last page, comment. The summary works out pages and pace as you type. If you reach the last page of the book, it asks whether you finished it. Manual sessions are added from the Session menu.
blog.l99.p_12: The history groups sessions by book in a tree with plus and minus, with five figures at the top: sessions, total time, pages, pages per minute and pages per day. Double tap a session to edit it, long press to delete it.
blog.l99.p_13: Statistics are a reading report in monospaced text, as if it came out of a printer: a summary with longest streak and average rating, time per book with block bars, speed in pages per day, a calendar of the year drawn in characters according to the pages read each day, and the last seven days.
blog.l99.p_14: Pagi travels to 1999 too. It is the same one-eyed bookmark silhouette, but pixelated, and it roams loose on the screen like the office assistants of that era. You drag it with your finger, it says a short line when you tap it and it changes expression depending on what you are doing: it thinks while you search for a book, reads while the timer runs and celebrates when you save a session or finish a book.
blog.l99.p_15: The app's tips appear in yellow balloons anchored to Pagi, once each. If you want to go over them again, they are under Help, in Tip of the day.
blog.l99.p_16: Lecturameter 1999 is simpler on purpose. It is an experiment and, in principle, it will not get any further development after release. New features will keep coming to Lecturameter.
blog.l99.p_17: While building it I decided that anything that didn't affect the reading flow was out. That's why Lecturameter 1999 has no Pro. What you see is what you get.
blog.l99.p_18: Lecturameter 1999 will ship in every language Lecturameter supports.
blog.l99.p_19: It will come to Play Store and App Store, free, after Lecturameter for iOS and version 3.7 are out. It is finished and running on my phone. Testing with my real library and the last details remain before publishing it. When it is available I will announce it here, on X and on Reddit.
blog.l99.p_20: In the meantime, Lecturameter is still Lecturameter, with its themes, its challenges and its bingos. The 1999 edition is another way of looking at the same data.

blog.hfr.title: How fast do I really read?
blog.hfr.description: Four months of tracked reading sessions. A real average pages per minute.
blog.hfr.og_description: Four months of tracked reading sessions. A real average pages per minute.
blog.hfr.tagline: Four months of tracked reading sessions. A real average pages per minute.
blog.hfr.p_01: I run Lecturameter, my own app, of course. Between May and September of this year I tracked 64 reading sessions with the app. Every session logs the pages I read, the minutes it took me and the book.
blog.hfr.p_03: People who don't track their readings might think that the average speed is mostly stable, but it's not. There are multiple variables: the language you're reading in, font size, physical vs digital format, how dense the prose is, how familiar you are with the subject, even the day of the week or the hour within the day.
blog.hfr.p_04: Saturday sessions are almost twice as fast as Sunday sessions. The data does not tell you why, but it tells the story on "how fast I read", which is because I was reading in a park with no distractions.
blog.hfr.p_05: The pace also changes with the book, like I said before. Let's go through the data:
blog.hfr.p_06: Same reader. 5x difference. One is dense fantasy prose. The other is a manga. Any average that mixes those two is a fiction that hides more than it explains, that's why every book and genre has its own stats, because a global stat can "lie".
blog.hfr.p_07: If you want to know how fast you read, do not read a paragraph and multiply. Time an actual session with an actual book. Do it a few times. Look at the individual numbers and then look the average, that way you'll have the bigger picture.
blog.hfr.p_08: If you own an Android phone, Lecturameter does this for you. If you do not, a stopwatch and a notebook do the same job. The tool matters less than the habit of timing yourself honestly. (and if you have an iPhone you'll soon be able to try Lecturameter!)
blog.hfr.p_09: The reading timer, the pace calculation and the daily and weekly breakdowns are the core of Lecturameter. It is free, it is Android and it does not need an account. You can take a look here.
blog.hfr.label_12: The Dragon Reborn · 37 sessions · 647 pages · 1023 min
blog.fvm.title: Fantasy vs manga: two completely different reading paces
blog.fvm.description: A real dataset of 64 tracked sessions. Fantasy averages 0.63 pages per minute. Manga hits 3.44. What that means when you plan your reading month.
blog.fvm.og_description: A real dataset of 64 tracked sessions. Fantasy averages 0.63 pages per minute. Manga hits 3.44.
blog.fvm.tagline: A real dataset of 64 tracked sessions. Fantasy averages 0.63 pages per minute. Manga hits 3.44. What that means when you plan your reading month.
blog.fvm.p_01: When people talk about reading pace they say things like "I read about a book a week". That is fine as a mood but useless as a plan, because a book a week for a manga reader and a book a week for a Sanderson reader are two universes.
blog.fvm.p_02: I have numbers now. Me, four months, 64 tracked reading sessions.
blog.fvm.p_03: You do not need statistics for that gap to matter. Manga sessions are roughly five times faster than fantasy sessions, per page. Which means:
blog.fvm.li_02: A fantasy session covers around 20 pages.
blog.fvm.p_04: The Dragon Reborn, book three of The Wheel of Time. 672 pages. 37 tracked sessions across 95 days. Average pace: 0.63 pages per minute. The five slowest sessions I recorded this year are all from this book.
blog.fvm.p_05: Hábito y mortaja, book two of a Spanish fantasy series. 450 tracked pages, 16 sessions. Average pace: 0.95 pages per minute. Faster prose, tighter chapters. You feel it in the pace.
blog.fvm.p_06: Frieren, Volume 1, manga. 165 pages, 2 sessions. Average pace: 3.44 pages per minute. The whole volume goes in less than an hour of real reading.
blog.fvm.p_07: Chainsaw Man tomos 21 to 24, four manga volumes. Every one of them started and finished the same day. Same for Dan Da Dan tomos 18 through 23. Six volumes, six same-day reads.
blog.fvm.p_08: When you plan a reading month, use the pace of the genre you are actually planning to read.
blog.fvm.p_09: If your next book is 800 pages of fantasy and you have 45 minutes a day, that is 45 x 0.8 pages per minute, so around 36 pages a day. Around three weeks and a half. This is real information you can use to determine what and how to read next.
blog.fvm.p_10: If your next book is a 200 page manga volume, that is one Sunday afternoon.
blog.fvm.p_11: The app remembers your average pace per book, not just overall. When you open the book screen you see "at your current pace, X hours to finish". The number is honest, because it is based on how you actually read that book, not a global average that mixes manga and Sanderson.
blog.fvm.p_12: Any tracker that gives you one single reading speed number is going to lie to you the moment you switch genres. What you want is a per-book pace and a per-session log, so you can spot the pattern.
blog.fvm.p_13: Lecturameter is a free reading tracker for Android with a proper reading timer. It logs sessions, calculates your real pace per book, and does not upload anything.
blog.rtp.title: Reading time or pages: which one should you track?
blog.rtp.description: Time and pages measure different things. Pages count output. Time counts effort. When you have both you get a pace, which is the useful part.
blog.rtp.og_description: Time and pages measure different things. Pages count output. Time counts effort. When you have both you get a pace.
blog.rtp.tagline: Time and pages measure different things. Pages count output. Time counts effort. When you have both you get a pace, which is the useful part.
blog.rtp.p_01: The two most common ways to track your reading are pages and time. Every reading app I have seen picks one and hides the other.
blog.rtp.p_02: Both are useful. They measure different things.
blog.rtp.p_03: Pages measure output. It is what you got done. It is how you finish a book.
blog.rtp.p_04: Time measures effort. It is what you spent. It is how you fit reading into your day.
blog.rtp.p_05: If you only track pages, your log looks like a productivity dashboard. Pages this week, pages this month, pages this year. Book count is a byproduct. It is clean and satisfying and it hides how long you actually sat with the book.
blog.rtp.p_06: Two people can both do 100 pages a day. One did it in 40 minutes on the train. The other did it in three hours on a Sunday. Same output, completely different lives.
blog.rtp.p_07: If you only track time, the log looks more like a habit tracker. Minutes today, streak this week, hours this month. It is closer to the truth of what happens, but it says nothing about what you were doing with those minutes. Ten minutes of manga and ten minutes of Wittgenstein are not the same ten minutes.
blog.rtp.p_08: Time plus pages gives you pace. Pages per minute. That is the number that actually says something about you as a reader today, with this book.
blog.rtp.p_09: Once you have pace you can:
blog.rtp.li_01: Predict how long a book will take at your current speed
blog.rtp.li_02: Compare genres without lying to yourself
blog.rtp.li_03: Notice when a book is dragging (your pace drops)
blog.rtp.li_04: Notice when a session was unusually good (your pace jumps)
blog.rtp.p_10: I have 64 sessions logged this year. The pace changes with the book. It changes with the day of the week. It changes over months. If I only tracked pages I would think I read faster on weekends. If I only tracked time I would think Sunday and Saturday were the same. Because I track both, I can see that Saturday sessions are almost twice as fast as Sunday sessions. Same person, same books, different attention.
blog.rtp.p_11: If you have to pick one, pick time. Pages are easy to remember and can be filled in later. Time is not. Once a session is over you cannot remember how long you spent. Time has to be measured while it happens or it is lost.
blog.rtp.p_12: If you can, track both. That is exactly what Lecturameter does. Start a session, read, stop. Enter the pages. You now have effort, output and pace, all three, without doing any math.
blog.rtp.p_13: The point of tracking anything is that you learn something from the data. Track only pages and you learn how much. Track only time and you learn how often. Track both and you learn about yourself.
blog.egl.title: How to bring your Goodreads (and StoryGraph, Bookmory, Fable…) library into Lecturameter
blog.egl.description: Lecturameter imports libraries from Goodreads, StoryGraph, Bookmory, Fable/ShelfBridge and other reading apps. Here is how each export works and what comes across.
blog.egl.og_description: Lecturameter imports libraries from Goodreads, StoryGraph, Bookmory, Fable/ShelfBridge and other reading apps. Here is how each export works.
blog.egl.tagline: Lecturameter reads exports from Goodreads, StoryGraph, Bookmory, Fable/ShelfBridge and several other reading apps. This post walks through each one.
blog.egl.p_01: If you already track your reading somewhere else and you want to move it, Lecturameter accepts exports from most of the popular tracking apps: Goodreads, StoryGraph, Bookmory, Fable (via the ShelfBridge extension) and a handful of smaller ones. This post covers the export step for each source, so you can pick the one you use and follow the steps.
blog.egl.p_02: Nothing here needs a Lecturameter account. The file lives on your phone.
blog.egl.p_03: When you open Lecturameter for the first time, Pagi asks what you want to do. One of the options is "I'm coming from another app". Pick that and you land on the import wizard.
blog.egl.p_04: The wizard is a list of sources. You tap the one you use, hand it the file, and Lecturameter reads the schema. Same wizard also lives in Settings, Import, so you can run it later.
blog.egl.p_05: Goodreads still lets you export your library, but the option is hidden and it only works from the desktop site. On mobile it is missing.
blog.egl.li_01: Go to goodreads.com and log in.
blog.egl.li_02: Click "My Books" in the top nav.
blog.egl.li_03: On the left sidebar, under "Tools", click "Import and export".
blog.egl.li_04: Look for the section "Export your books" and click "Export Library".
blog.egl.li_05: Wait a minute. When the file is ready you see a link like "Your export from Goodreads" that downloads a CSV.
blog.egl.p_06: The file is one row per book with around thirty columns. What matters: title, author, ISBN, your rating, dates read, dates added, shelves (custom and exclusive) and your review text. Private notes come across in the "Private Notes" column, which is easy to miss.
blog.egl.p_07: The rating uses whole stars, not half stars. Dates are in "YYYY/MM/DD" format. Friends, comments, likes and groups stay on Goodreads. That is not a Lecturameter limitation, they simply are not in the file.
blog.egl.p_08: StoryGraph exports from the web too. Go to app.thestorygraph.com, open Settings, then Manage Account, and use the Export option. You get a CSV with your books, shelves, ratings, review text, dates and tags. Lecturameter reads it directly and maps the fields.
blog.egl.p_09: Inside Bookmory open Settings, then Backup, then "Export to Excel". You get an .xlsx with separate sheets for books, ratings and reading sessions. Lecturameter reads the xlsx directly; you do not need to convert it.
blog.egl.p_10: Fable itself does not have an export button. The community project ShelfBridge is a browser extension that reads your Fable data and produces a Fable-compatible CSV. Lecturameter accepts that file in the Fable / ShelfBridge slot of the wizard.
blog.egl.p_11: Open Book Tracker, go to Settings > Export and pick CSV. You get a file with your books, ratings, dates and shelves. Drop it in the Book Tracker slot of the wizard and Lecturameter reads it.
blog.egl.p_12: The wizard also has an "Other apps" slot for Babelio, Pagebound, Bookshelf, Delibrista and similar. If the app you use can produce a CSV or an XLSX, Lecturameter tries to detect the schema automatically.
blog.egl.p_13: If yours is not recognised, the fallback is easy: open the file in a spreadsheet, keep the columns for title, author, rating, dates and shelf, save it as CSV, and import it as Goodreads. The Goodreads reader is the most permissive of the lot.
blog.egl.h2_09: What comes across, what does not
blog.egl.p_14: For all sources, the same things travel: books, shelves, ratings, dates and personal notes or reviews.
blog.egl.p_15: The same things stay behind on every service too: friends, comments, likes, groups and follows. That is a limitation of the export files themselves, not of Lecturameter. There is nothing to bring across because they were never in the file.
blog.egl.p_16: If you skipped the wizard on first launch, the import also lives in Settings, Import. It reads the shelves in your file and asks which ones you want to bring across. Ratings, dates and notes come with the books. Nothing goes to a server. Your library ends up on your phone.
